I’ve put together a maths proof – would anyone like to take a look at the problem?
Unfortunately, I think an AI may have mislead you to think you have proven things that maybe are less meaningful than you intended. And there is no context.
In fact, these ideas were first conceived by me and other humans, and then written up using AI.
There just is no context to even know if you proved what you wanted to or not is the bigger issue right now, at least in your post.

Even reading the read me, I am left rather puzzled, but if you want to share broader interest you might want to put some of that in the description too of the post too.

Disclaimer in that I do not endorse you posting this or the veracity of the post, in no offensive way to you, but if it is to exist right now -- might as well make it more inviting.

Thank you, you make a valid point. I’ll update the README, but what puzzles me is this: if you pose a mathematical problem and prove that it has never been asked before, how would you know that it is a significant problem? This is precisely the difficulty I’m facing at the moment. I’m a philosopher, and this proof is a mathematical one driven by philosophical thought, but I’m unsure how to apply the traditional criteria for judging a problem within such a new field.
By the way, this repository of mine contains PDFs of papers I’ve written; if you’re interested, you’re welcome to have a read and review them.

Haha, you just stumbled upon a rather deep and strange part of math academia. Indeed you are right, especially in pure math, what is simply novel, and what do these people find interesting?

Unfortunately the answer I have arrived to is rather unsatisfactory, but you are right in seeing this tension. For instance, I could maybe conceive and contrive a very specific integral , that perhaps no one has solved or MENTIONED before. Then solve it. It is novel, but people would not be overly excited.

The key is in MENTIONED, it appears to be a system running under its own momentum over time, where the "greats" write math, and others can then often justify novel things if its something those "greats" have mentioned, and if they do this well enough they become the next "great".

At that stage they are freed to do whatever really and its considered interesting, restarting the cycle. This is just my view though.

I think I just realised reading that back, that is perhaps simply how trying to get the interest and attention of any community works at its core, but perhaps pure math abstraction and divorcing from reality enhances the subjective element of this.

As opposed to some research that's novel and concretely about reality, that by that virtue is more likely to be of "inherent" interest.

End of the day, you don't need them to do math that interests you, and perhaps you'll find its a "never meet your heros" scenario like I did, where even plenty professional mathematicians end up nothing like you thought if you met them and engaged them on why they do maths and how.

The biggest benefit to such a thing, would be the mentorship and teaching from people who know and are more experienced, but often that is the very thing they won't do, as they too are seeking those who can teach them and gain, rather than be the teacher and purely share.

I believe there are some profound insights in what you’ve said.

There is a marvellous connection between the repository of human knowledge and human ideas; a simple idea must be embraced by the entirety of human knowledge and become a stable node before its value can circulate. I recall seeing a lecture by Friedman that conveyed a similar point. Novel ideas attract more attention because they are sufficiently interesting; those with potential for development are then expanded upon and retained, whilst those that are merely sensationalist are discarded.

However, on a slightly different note, I believe there are still many issues with the ‘firewall’ of the human knowledge base; sometimes hackers can breach it. The biggest ‘hacker’ at present is AI, which has left behind a great deal of redundant and meaningless content. As for the issue of integration, I am actually quite interested. What exactly constitutes a new method of integration?

Moreover, isn’t integration concerned with time and space? If your approach is truly novel and derived from first principles, I think it would be fascinating. I believe that any mathematical system derived from first principles will be of value.

In the past, it might have taken several hundred years for such ideas to be incorporated into the network of knowledge and value, but in future this process may be accelerated, aided by AI in identifying and utilising them.

You’re quite right—one shouldn’t blindly follow authority; that’s something a PhD holder once told me too. In truth, I don’t idolise mathematics mentors; I respect them, but I don’t regard them as great figures or authorities. At heart, I’m a philosopher, and I know that we’re only human. The part of mathematics that humanity has understood is merely a garden; beyond it lie grasslands, thickets of thorns and the vast ocean. I recall Friedman saying that the capacity for understanding required in mathematics is double-exponential—I can’t remember the exact figures—but many mathematical spaces are not user-friendly for humans and lie beyond our capacity for comprehension, just as one cannot swim across the Pacific Ocean unaided. This leaves me feeling a little disheartened, but I believe that ‘mathematical luxury yachts’ will eventually emerge, ha ha.

Mathematicians are all obsessed with games and love to explore problems, so they tend to view teaching others as a waste of time. However, human development also involves cultural exchange beyond the mere transfer of knowledge. I feel that this aspect does not require too much time spent on formal instruction, but rather the companionship and encouragement that comes from simply ‘being there’. Unfortunately, such mathematical mentors are in short supply. My own mathematical ethos is that it is one’s own responsibility to research the mathematical problems one loves.

Among my own papers, some solve a problem posed by other people, while others exhibit more "original thinking". Generally speaking, I like the latter papers more, but they're also harder to get published. Therefore, I am sympathetic to some of the concerns expressed in this thread. However, I think the thing to do is not to complain, but to work harder to provide motivation for your "original work."

Nothing is ever completely original. Therefore you need to establish a connection between your work and the prior work of others. Even if you're not directly answering someone else's question, you're probably presenting a new way to look at an old subject, or posing new questions about familiar objects. It's your job to make it clear what advantages your ideas have over the conventional ideas. Novelty for the sake of novelty is unlikely to interest many people.

I would like to point out that, whilst we naturally update our knowledge based on experience, what truly matters is determining which problems are valuable and which are worth solving.

In other words, what you are describing is a judgement of value based on what humanity deems meaningful, but what does this process of determining meaning actually entail? What is the difference in value between a good problem and a good interpretation? I believe this is the question humanity must answer in the face of the disruption brought about by AI.

My view is that if a first-rate mathematician wastes time on second-rate problems, they will, at best, become a second-rate problem-solver; but the true value lies in a first-rate mathematician creating and breaking new ground with genuinely first-rate mathematical problems.

The key question, however, is: on the frontiers of the unknown, how can one know whether a novel solution is of value?

I think the most important quality is still being honest with oneself. Admitting that a maths problem has been a waste of time is certainly frustrating, but it allows you to focus your attention on the problems that really matter.
